config.title: Test Async Component

intro.title: Test Async Component
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that fetches and displays data from a mock API. You'll learn how to test asynchronous behavior in React components using React Testing Library and Jest. The main technologies involved are React, TypeScript, and async/await for handling promises. This will help you understand how to write reliable tests for components that load data asynchronously.
intro.usecase: Testing async components is essential for building reliable React applications that fetch and display data from APIs. In real-world products like e-commerce dashboards, social media feeds, or financial tracking apps, components frequently load user data, product listings, or transaction histories asynchronously. Developers must verify these components correctly handle loading states, display fetched data, and manage errors to prevent broken user experiences. Proper async testing ensures your UI remains responsive and trustworthy when network requests succeed, fail, or take longer than expected.

objectives: Initialize a state variable to manage asynchronous data loading status
Implement a handler function to simulate fetching data with a delay
Apply conditional rendering to display loading, error, and success UI states
Integrate a button component that triggers the asynchronous data fetch
Configure a cleanup mechanism to prevent state updates on unmounted components
Manipulate the component's UI to reflect the resolved data from the async operation
Construct a test that verifies the component's behavior during asynchronous interactions

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing from a package
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the necessary imports to use React components and state management.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Define the main component
steps.instruction: Define a functional component named TestAsyncComponent with no props. Return null for now.
steps.hint: Create a function or arrow function called TestAsyncComponent that returns null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Define TestAsyncComponent here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named TestAsyncComponent is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: TestAsyncComponent is defined as a function or arrow function and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined the TestAsyncComponent component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You defined a component, but make sure it's named exactly TestAsyncComponent and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check the name and return value.

steps.title: Initialize loading state
steps.instruction: Inside your component, initialize a loading state variable using useState. Set its default value to false.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The state variable should be a boolean.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a boolean state
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a loading state variable (e.g., isLoading) initialized to false, ready to track whether an async operation is in progress.
successCriteria: The component contains a useState call that initializes a boolean state variable with the value false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added state, but check: is it a boolean with default value false? Make sure you're using useState correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading state isn't initialized yet. Use useState to create a boolean state variable with default value false inside the component.

steps.title: Initialize data state
steps.instruction: Inside your TestAsyncComponent, initialize a data state variable using useState with a default value of null. Use TypeScript to type it as string | null.
steps.hint: Add a second useState call after your loading state. The type annotation should be <string | null>.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: state for fetched data
const [data, setData] = useState<string | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: loading (boolean) and data (string | null).
successCriteria: A data state variable is declared with useState
It has a default value of null
It is typed as string | null using TypeScript generics
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to type the state as string | null and set the default to null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added a second useState call with the correct type and default value.

steps.title: Define the async fetch handler
steps.instruction: Inside your TestAsyncComponent, define an async function named fetchData that simulates an API call. The function should not take any parameters and should return a Promise.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before the function declaration. Inside the function, you can simulate a delay using setTimeout or Promise.resolve.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an async function named fetchData defined inside your component, ready to be called later.
successCriteria: The async function fetchData is defined inside TestAsyncComponent and returns a Promise.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the function is async and named fetchData.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've defined an async function named fetchData inside the component.

steps.title: Set loading state in fetch handler
steps.instruction: Inside your fetchData function, set the loading state to true at the beginning of the function before the async fetch call.
steps.hint: Use the setLoading state setter function with the value true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function should now set loading to true when called, indicating the async operation has started.
successCriteria: The fetchData function contains setLoading(true) as its first statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure setLoading(true) is the first statement in fetchData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading state isn't being set correctly. Add setLoading(true) at the beginning of fetchData.

steps.title: Update data state in fetch handler
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchData function, after setting loading to true, add an await statement to simulate fetching data,
steps.hint: Use await with a Promise that resolves after a short delay, then call setData with a mock object (like { message: 'Data loaded!' }) and setLoading(false).
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function now simulates an async operation, updates the data state with mock data, and properly manages the loading state.
successCriteria: The fetchData function includes an await statement, updates data state with a mock object, and resets loading to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to include both the data update and loading reset in your fetchData function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that your fetchData function simulates an async delay, updates the data state, and sets loading back to false.

steps.instruction: update the data state with a mock response and set loading back to false.
steps.hint: Use await with a Promise that resolves after a short delay, then call setData with a mock object (like { message: 'Data loaded!' }) and setLoading(false).
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Create the component structure
steps.instruction: Return a div container with a heading that says 'Async Data Fetcher' from your TestAsyncComponent.
steps.hint: Replace the current return null; with a JSX structure that includes a div and an h1 element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a JSX structure with a div container and an h1 heading.
successCriteria: The component returns a div element
The div contains an h1 element with the text 'Async Data Fetcher'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're returning a div with an h1 inside it that says 'Async Data Fetcher'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a JSX structure with a div container and an h1 heading. Try replacing 'return null;' with the appropriate JSX.

steps.title: Add fetch button and wire handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside your component's return statement that calls the fetchData function when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the onClick prop on a button element to call your fetchData function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button with click handler
<button onClick={() => console.log('Clicked')}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button element appears in the component's return statement with an onClick handler that calls fetchData.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have a button element with an onClick handler that calls fetchData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or onClick handler is missing. Add a button element that calls fetchData when clicked.
